<reason>PRO (B) built the more complete comparative case: the incentive asymmetry, lateral spread of fear, and the visible-versus-invisible asymmetry formed a coherent framework for why self-censorship does more damage "now." CON's best weapon was the symmetry turn—if fear can hollow out assessment of omissions, it can also shield entrenched falsehoods—which genuinely pressured PRO's assumption that visible bad content gets corrected. But PRO absorbed it in the closing by arguing that visible content carries external evidence (courts, parents, ballots, as in Dover) that omission never generates, and flipped CON's own Dover example into "my best witness." CON also never established the prevalence of genuinely harmful curriculum, leaving its positive case thin, while its definitional critique ("PRO wins by definition") was answered head-on by distinguishing accuracy review from discomfort policing. PRO answered both pressure questions directly, handled the Dover concession with the hammer analogy, and closed by narrowing the dispute to "which threat can be fought," the cleanest decision rule offered by either side. CON was precise and honest but mostly defensive, needing PRO's oversight asymmetry to collapse entirely and never quite making it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive sequence was CON's symmetry attack ([A4.5]: PRO cannot make institutions politically vulnerable on omissions yet politically reliable on falsehoods) met by PRO's embrace-and-flip in the closing ([B5.4]-[B5.5]): the fear that silences teaching also silences the test question, while visible falsehood still leaves a trail for courts, voters, and parents—turning CON's Dover concession into PRO's strongest evidence.</best_rebuttal>
